title: The Psychology of Colour
context:
Colour influences how we feel more than most of us realise, yet scientists caution that the effects are smaller and more complicated than popular books claim. The perception of colour begins in the retina, where three types of cone cells respond to red, green and blue light. The brain combines their signals to create the full range of shades that we see. About one in twelve men has a form of colour blindness, usually involving difficulty in distinguishing red from green, compared with roughly one in two hundred women. Colour vision is also not perfectly stable: the same shirt can look blue in daylight and purple under a lamp, because the brain adjusts for the light around it.

Many studies have examined the link between colour and emotion. Red is associated in several cultures with danger and excitement, and one well-known study found that athletes wearing red in combat sports won slightly more often than those wearing blue. Critics note that the effect is small and may depend on the sport, the referees and the audience. Blue, in contrast, is often described as calming, and it is the most frequently chosen favourite colour in surveys carried out across many different countries.

Cultural differences matter greatly. White is the colour of weddings in much of Europe, but in parts of East Asia it is traditionally worn at funerals. Green signifies luck in Ireland, while in some other places it is linked to illness or envy. Language may shape perception as well. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and Russian speakers have been shown to distinguish between the two shades slightly faster than English speakers, who use a single word for both.

Businesses make use of colour constantly. Fast food chains often use red and yellow, which are thought to stimulate appetite and create a sense of urgency, while banks favour blue to convey stability and trust. Evidence for such effects is limited, though. Brand colours seem to work chiefly by making a company recognisable, and consistency matters more than any particular shade. In hospitals, designers choose soft greens and blues to reduce anxiety, although the benefits are hard to separate from other aspects of the environment such as noise and lighting.

Colour may also affect performance. Some experiments suggest that exposure to red before a test can reduce results, perhaps because the colour is linked with failure through teachers' red pens. Other studies find that a view of green nature improves concentration and creativity. Replication has proved difficult for many colour studies, and researchers now emphasise larger samples and more careful controls. The emerging consensus is that colour acts as a subtle cue rather than a powerful force, and that context decides its meaning. This does not make colour unimportant to designers; it means that its effects are usually modest and easily overwhelmed by shape, texture and meaning.
